Monarch (Danaus plexippus) "Wing Span: 3 3/8 - 4 7/8 inches (8.6 - 12.4 cm). Identification: Upperside of male is bright orange with wide black borders and black veins; hindwing has a patch of scent scales. Upperside of female is orange-brown with wide black borders and blurred black veins. Both sexes have white spots on borders and apex. The Viceroy butterfly (Limenitis archippus) is a Mullerian mimic; it has similar coloration and is also distasteful. Life History: Adults warm up by basking dorsally (with their wings open and toward the sun). Females lay eggs singly under the host leaves; caterpillars eat leaves and flowers. Adults make massive migrations from August-October, flying thousands of miles south to hibernate along the California coast and in central Mexico. A few overwinter along the Gulf coast or south Atlantic coast. Along the way, Monarchs stop to feed on flower nectar and to roost together at night. At the Mexico wintering sites, butterflies roost in trees and form huge aggregations that may have millions of individuals. During the winter the butterflies may take moisture and flower nectar during warm days. Most have mated before they leave for the north in the spring, and females lay eggs along the way. Residents of tropical areas do not migrate but appear to make altitude changes during the dry season. Flight: In North America during spring and summer there may be 1-3 broods in the north and 4-6 broods in the south. May breed all year in Florida, South Texas, and southeastern California. Caterpillar Hosts: Milkweeds including Rush Milkweed (Asclepas subdulata) in the Coachella Valley, Common Milkweed (Asclepias syriaca), Swamp Milkweed (A. incarnata), and Showy Milkweed (A. speciosa), and milkweed vine in the tropics. Most milkweeds contain cardiac glycosides which are stored in the bodies of both the caterpillar and adult. These poisons are distasteful and emetic to birds and other vertebrate predators. After tasting a Monarch, a predator might associate the bright warning colors of the adult or caterpillar with an unpleasant meal, and avoid Monarchs in the future. Adult Food: Nectar from all milkweeds. Early in the season before milkweeds bloom, Monarchs visit a variety of flowers including dogbane, lilac, red clover, lantana, and thistles. In the fall adults visit composites including goldenrods, blazing stars, ironweed, and tickseed sunflower. Habitat: Many open habitats including fields, meadows, weedy areas, marshes, and roadsides. Range: Southern Canada south through all of the United States, Central America, and most of South America. Also present in Australia, Hawaii, and other Pacific Islands. Conservation: Overwintering sites in California and Mexico should be protected and conserved." Brock and Kaufman, 2003, pp. 226-227. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Tiger Milkweed Butterflies (Danaus) genus observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=48663&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 Butterflies of the genus Danaus (monarchs, queens, tigers, wanderers) are globally distributed milkweed butterflies recognized for their bright orange-and-black aposematic coloration, chemical defense from milkweed toxins, and in some species, long-distance migrations. They comprise about a dozen species across the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Australia. The genus includes 12–13 recognized species found worldwide, with centers of diversity in North and South America, Africa, and Asia. Well-known representatives include the Monarch (Danaus plexippus), Queen (D. gilippus), Plain Tiger (D. chrysippus), and Common Tiger (D. genutia). Species occupy habitats ranging from tropical lowlands to temperate grasslands, depending on the availability of milkweed (Asclepiadoideae) host plants. Most species show orange to reddish wings with black veins and borders, often with white spots, a classic aposematic signal warning predators of toxicity. Males often have androconial patches (scent scales) on the hindwings used in courtship. Wingspans typically range from 7–12 cm, with the Monarch among the largest. Caterpillars are banded in black, white, and yellow, with pairs of fleshy filaments at both ends. Larvae feed on milkweeds, sequestering cardenolides (cardiac glycosides). These compounds render both larvae and adults toxic or unpalatable to vertebrate predators. Bright coloration functions as a warning signal, reinforced by predator learning. The Monarch is unique for its multi-generational, long-distance migration (up to 3,000 km) between North America and overwintering sites in Mexico or coastal California. Other species, such as D. erippus in South America, show regional movements but not the same scale of migration. Females lay eggs singly on milkweed leaves; larvae undergo complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult). The genus belongs to family Nymphalidae (brush-footed butterflies), tribe Danaini (milkweed butterflies), with authority Kluk, 1802. Historically divided into subgenera (Danaus, Anosia, Salatura), it is now treated as a single genus. Adults visit a wide range of nectar sources, aiding pollination. Monarch declines highlight broader threats to pollinators from habitat loss, pesticides, and climate change. Danaus species participate in Müllerian mimicry rings, where multiple toxic species share similar warning patterns, reinforcing predator avoidance. In sum, Danaus butterflies are defined by milkweed dependence, chemical defense, warning coloration, and in some cases, spectacular migration, serving as both ecological keystones and flagship species for conservation. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Brush-footed Butterflies (Nymphalidae) family observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=47922&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 Brush-footed Butterflies, a.k.a. Four-footed Butterflies, (Nymphalidae) are the largest family of butterflies, with over 6,000 species worldwide. Members range from medium to large size and belong to the Papilionoidea superfamily. Commonly known as brush-footed or four-footed butterflies, this group includes familiar forms such as Monarchs, Admirals, Emperors and Fritillaries. Brush-footed Butterflies display a large diversity of colors and patterns across its many subfamilies. Adults are distinguished by a markedly reduced first pair of legs—which are often tufted with brush-like hairs—and are held curled against the body, so that the butterfly effectively stands on only four legs. Many species hold their vividly colored upper wings flat when at rest, while the undersides are typically duller or cryptically leaf-like. Identification: Upperside of male is bright orange with wide black borders and black veins; hindwing has a patch of scent scales. Upperside of female is orange-brown with wide black borders and blurred black veins. Both sexes have white spots on borders and apex. The Viceroy butterfly (Limenitis archippus) is a Mullerian mimic; it has similar coloration and is also distasteful. Life History: Adults warm up by basking dorsally (with their wings open and toward the sun). Females lay eggs singly under the host leaves; caterpillars eat leaves and flowers. Adults make massive migrations from August-October, flying thousands of miles south to hibernate along the California coast and in central Mexico. A few overwinter along the Gulf coast or south Atlantic coast. Along the way, Monarchs stop to feed on flower nectar and to roost together at night. At the Mexico wintering sites, butterflies roost in trees and form huge aggregations that may have millions of individuals. During the winter the butterflies may take moisture and flower nectar during warm days. Most have mated before they leave for the north in the spring, and females lay eggs along the way. Residents of tropical areas do not migrate but appear to make altitude changes during the dry season. The genus includes 12–13 recognized species found worldwide, with centers of diversity in North and South America, Africa, and Asia. Danaus species participate in Müllerian mimicry rings, where multiple toxic species share similar warning patterns, reinforcing predator avoidance. Brock and Kaufman, 2003, pp. 226-227 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Tiger Milkweed Butterflies (Danaus) genus observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=48663&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 "Butterflies of the genus Danaus (monarchs, queens, tigers, wanderers) are globally distributed milkweed butterflies recognized for their bright orange-and-black coloration, chemical defense from milkweed toxins, and in some species, long-distance migrations. The genus includes 12–13 recognized species found worldwide, with centers of diversity in North and South America, Africa, and Asia. Well-known representatives include the Monarch (Danaus plexippus), Queen (D. gilippus), Plain Tiger (D. chrysippus), and Common Tiger (D. genutia). Species occupy habitats ranging from tropical lowlands to temperate grasslands, depending on the availability of milkweed (Asclepiadoideae) host plants. Most species show orange to reddish wings with black veins and borders, often with white spots, a classic aposematic signal warning predators of toxicity. Males often have androconial patches (scent scales) on the hindwings used in courtship. Wingspans typically range from 7–12 cm, with the Monarch among the largest. Caterpillars are banded in black, white, and yellow, with pairs of fleshy filaments at both ends. Larvae feed on milkweeds, sequestering cardenolides (cardiac glycosides). These compounds render both larvae and adults toxic or unpalatable to vertebrate predators. Bright coloration functions as a warning signal, reinforced by predator learning. The Monarch is unique for its multi-generational, long-distance migration (up to 3,000 km) between North America and overwintering sites in Mexico or coastal California. Other species, such as D. erippus in South America, show regional movements but not the same scale of migration. Females lay eggs singly on milkweed leaves; larvae undergo complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult). The genus belongs to family Nymphalidae (brush-footed butterflies), tribe Danaini (milkweed butterflies). Historically divided into subgenera (Danaus, Anosia, Salatura), it is now treated as a single genus. Adults visit a wide range of nectar sources, aiding pollination. Monarch declines highlight broader threats to pollinators from habitat loss, pesticides, and climate change. Danaus species participate in Müllerian mimicry rings, where multiple toxic species share similar warning patterns, reinforcing predator avoidance. In sum, Danaus butterflies are defined by milkweed dependence, chemical defense, warning coloration, and in some cases, spectacular migration, serving as both ecological keystones and flagship species for conservation." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Brush-footed Butterflies (Nymphalidae) family observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=47922&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 Brush-footed Butterflies, a.k.a. Commonly known as brush-footed or four-footed butterflies, this group includes familiar forms such as Monarchs, Admirals, Emperors and Fritillaries. Monarch (Danaus plexippus) "Wing Span: 3 3/8 - 4 7/8 inches (8.6 - 12.4 cm). Identification: Upperside of male is bright orange with wide black borders and black veins; hindwing has a patch of scent scales. Upperside of female is orange-brown with wide black borders and blurred black veins. Both sexes have white spots on borders and apex. The Viceroy butterfly (Limenitis archippus) is a Mullerian mimic; it has similar coloration and is also distasteful. Life History: Adults warm up by basking dorsally (with their wings open and toward the sun). Females lay eggs singly under the host leaves; caterpillars eat leaves and flowers. Adults make massive migrations from August-October, flying thousands of miles south to hibernate along the California coast and in central Mexico. A few overwinter along the Gulf coast or south Atlantic coast. Along the way, Monarchs stop to feed on flower nectar and to roost together at night. At the Mexico wintering sites, butterflies roost in trees and form huge aggregations that may have millions of individuals. During the winter the butterflies may take moisture and flower nectar during warm days. Most have mated before they leave for the north in the spring, and females lay eggs along the way. Residents of tropical areas do not migrate but appear to make altitude changes during the dry season. Flight: In North America during spring and summer there may be 1-3 broods in the north and 4-6 broods in the south. May breed all year in Florida, South Texas, and southeastern California. Caterpillar Hosts: Milkweeds including Rush Milkweed (Asclepas subdulata) in the Coachella Valley, Common Milkweed (Asclepias syriaca), Swamp Milkweed (A. incarnata), and Showy Milkweed (A. speciosa), and milkweed vine in the tropics. Most milkweeds contain cardiac glycosides which are stored in the bodies of both the caterpillar and adult. These poisons are distasteful and emetic to birds and other vertebrate predators. After tasting a Monarch, a predator might associate the bright warning colors of the adult or caterpillar with an unpleasant meal, and avoid Monarchs in the future. Adult Food: Nectar from all milkweeds. Early in the season before milkweeds bloom, Monarchs visit a variety of flowers including dogbane, lilac, red clover, lantana, and thistles. In the fall adults visit composites including goldenrods, blazing stars, ironweed, and tickseed sunflower. Habitat: Many open habitats including fields, meadows, weedy areas, marshes, and roadsides. Range: Southern Canada south through all of the United States, Central America, and most of South America. Also present in Australia, Hawaii, and other Pacific Islands. Conservation: Overwintering sites in California and Mexico should be protected and conserved." Brock and Kaufman, 2003, pp. 226-227. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Tiger Milkweed Butterflies (Danaus) genus observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=48663&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 Butterflies of the genus Danaus (monarchs, queens, tigers, wanderers) are globally distributed milkweed butterflies recognized for their bright orange-and-black aposematic coloration, chemical defense from milkweed toxins, and in some species, long-distance migrations. They comprise about a dozen species across the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Australia. The genus includes 12–13 recognized species found worldwide, with centers of diversity in North and South America, Africa, and Asia. Well-known representatives include the Monarch (Danaus plexippus), Queen (D. gilippus), Plain Tiger (D. chrysippus), and Common Tiger (D. genutia). Species occupy habitats ranging from tropical lowlands to temperate grasslands, depending on the availability of milkweed (Asclepiadoideae) host plants. Most species show orange to reddish wings with black veins and borders, often with white spots, a classic aposematic signal warning predators of toxicity. Males often have androconial patches (scent scales) on the hindwings used in courtship. Wingspans typically range from 7–12 cm, with the Monarch among the largest. Caterpillars are banded in black, white, and yellow, with pairs of fleshy filaments at both ends. Larvae feed on milkweeds, sequestering cardenolides (cardiac glycosides). These compounds render both larvae and adults toxic or unpalatable to vertebrate predators. Bright coloration functions as a warning signal, reinforced by predator learning. The Monarch is unique for its multi-generational, long-distance migration (up to 3,000 km) between North America and overwintering sites in Mexico or coastal California. Other species, such as D. erippus in South America, show regional movements but not the same scale of migration. Females lay eggs singly on milkweed leaves; larvae undergo complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult). The genus belongs to family Nymphalidae (brush-footed butterflies), tribe Danaini (milkweed butterflies), with authority Kluk, 1802. Historically divided into subgenera (Danaus, Anosia, Salatura), it is now treated as a single genus. Adults visit a wide range of nectar sources, aiding pollination. Monarch declines highlight broader threats to pollinators from habitat loss, pesticides, and climate change. Danaus species participate in Müllerian mimicry rings, where multiple toxic species share similar warning patterns, reinforcing predator avoidance. In sum, Danaus butterflies are defined by milkweed dependence, chemical defense, warning coloration, and in some cases, spectacular migration, serving as both ecological keystones and flagship species for conservation. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Brush-footed Butterflies (Nymphalidae) family observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=47922&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 Brush-footed Butterflies, a.k.a. Four-footed Butterflies, (Nymphalidae) are the largest family of butterflies, with over 6,000 species worldwide. Members range from medium to large size and belong to the Papilionoidea superfamily. Commonly known as brush-footed or four-footed butterflies, this group includes familiar forms such as Monarchs, Admirals, Emperors and Fritillaries. Brush-footed Butterflies display a large diversity of colors and patterns across its many subfamilies. Adults are distinguished by a markedly reduced first pair of legs—which are often tufted with brush-like hairs—and are held curled against the body, so that the butterfly effectively stands on only four legs. Many species hold their vividly colored upper wings flat when at rest, while the undersides are typically duller or cryptically leaf-like.
